messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: identification error with second-order cfa
parts:
You are relying on cfa function defaults (mainly, fixing the first loading for each common factor to 1) to make the model identified.  The function may not be realizing that you also want this default to apply to stress.  The simplest fix might be to constrain the first loading on stress to 1:
 stress=~1*demand+emodemand+ethical+control+social+insecurity
     If that doesn't work, then you may need to get more elaborate.  You could:
--constrain the variance of stress to 1 (to scale it)--
stress ~~ 1*stress
--give stress an observed variable indicator, but with a 0 loading (so stress looks like a common factor)--
stress=~0*emotion5
--change the syntax of your last line so that stress is just predicting the other common factors:
demand+emodemand+ethical+control+social+insecurity~stress
--Ed Rigdon

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: identification error with second-order cfa
parts: I have tried all of the solutions but none of them seem to work....

I don't think this is causing your identification problem, but in your original post, you made an error:

cfa(model151020_3, data=data151020_3, bootstrap="se")

The bootstrap option takes an integer (default is 1000L), not a character string.  I am guessing you meant to ask for bootstrapped SEs, which would necessitate the se argument:

cfa(model151020_3, data=data151020_3, se = "bootstrap")

Because bootstrapping takes up some time, I would first leave out that option and just try to get your model to run in the first place.  Does the first-order CFA run (without a second-order factor)?

model151020_3 <- '
emotion =~ emotion1 + emotion2 + emotion3 + emotion4 + emotion5
beh =~ alc1 + smk1
demand =~ demand1 + demand2 + demand3 + demand3 + demand4
emodemand =~ emodemand1 + emodemand2 + emodemand3
ethical =~ ethical1 + ethical2 + ethical3
control =~ control2 + control3 + control4 + control5 + control6
social =~ social1 + social2 + social3 + social4 + social5
insecurity =~ insecurity1 + insecurity2 + insecurity3
'

Are the data continuous?  Are there missing data?  If a similar model runs after removing some latent variables, I'm more inclined to think it is a model misspecification problem that an "error of the data".  Make sure your first-order CFA runs and fits well, and only posit a second order factor if the first-order factor correlations are all quite high (e.g., 0.70 or so), indicating that they might actually be measuring/representing the same thing.

Terry

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: identification error with second-order cfa
parts:
Well, seeing your data cleared up a few things -- that's why it is so important to provide information to reproduce the problem.   You do NOT have all continuous variables.  Some are binary, and a few of the ordered variables have fewer than 5 categories, which is the situation when you should really treat them as ordinal data:

http://psycnet.apa.org/psycinfo/2012-18631-001/

In addition to the warning about being unable to compute standard errors, lavaan issues a warning telling you that there was a negative residual variance, and to inspect the theta matrix.  Doing so would have shown you that the residual variance for insecurity3 was negative, which is often a good clue about the source of identification, (mis)specification, or estimation troubles.  The standardized solution helps reveal which indicators do not seem to "go with the rest" of the indicators for it's factor.  The indicators of insecurity, demand, emodemand, and ethical have either very low or altogether inconsistent intercorrelations (using Kendall's tau instead of Pearson correlation, since they are not continuous, or are very non-normal even when approximately continuous), so you need to question whether they really measure the same thing.  You provided N = 2000 data points, so I don't think sampling error is much of an issue here, and your sample size is large enough to have no fear of using the more appropriate DWLS estimator and declaring at least the binary variables as categorical (which DOES converge and provide standard errors). 

You can see how I found this information in the attached R script, which includes some helpful basic data screening syntax.  In it, I calculated alc1 and smk1 by dividing by an arbitrary number to reduce their variances, but it probably isn't the same thing you did (which I didn't see evidence of in your previous posts).

Terry
